title: Therapy During Pregnancy: New Research Suggests Benefits for Mom and Baby
summary: New research suggests therapy during pregnancy may benefit mom and baby. Learn what the study found and how to find the right therapist for you.
body_markdown:
## How to Find a Therapist During Pregnancy


Finding the right support may feel like one more task on an already long list. However, a few simple steps can make the search easier, so you can find someone who feels like a good fit for this season of life.


#### Look for the Right Credentials


Many licensed mental health professionals can provide therapy during pregnancy. Common credentials include:


- **Psychologist (PhD or PsyD)** : Holds a doctoral degree and is trained in therapy and psychological testing.
- **Licensed clinical social worker (LCSW or LISW)** : Provides therapy with a focus on the person’s wider life, including family, work, and community support.
- **Licensed professional counselor (LPC, LPCC, or LMHC)** : Helps with stress, anxiety, depression, and life changes.
- **Licensed marriage and family therapist (LMFT)** : Specializes in relationships, which can be especially helpful as a family grows.


Some therapists also hold a perinatal mental health certification (PMH-C), which shows extra training in the emotional ups and downs of pregnancy and the months after birth. To understand the full range of[therapist credentials](https://lifestance.com/blog/therapist-types-credentials-explained-guide/) , it can also help to prepare a few[questions to ask a therapist](https://lifestance.com/blog/questions-to-ask-therapist-to-ensure-compatibility/) before the first session, such as how they approach pregnancy-related stress and what a typical session looks like.


#### Consider Bringing Your Partner or Family Along


Therapy during pregnancy doesn’t have to be a solo journey. Pregnancy changes the whole household, from who handles late-night feedings to how partners share the growing to-do list.[Couples therapy](https://lifestance.com/services/couples-therapy/) can give partners a calm space to talk through those shifts before the baby arrives, while[family therapy](https://lifestance.com/blog/family-therapy-benefits/) can help older children, grandparents, or other loved ones adjust to the changes ahead. Every conversation that eases stress at home may help create a steadier start for mom and baby alike.


#### Choose In-Person, Online, or Both


Today, therapy can fit around a busy pregnancy in more ways than one. In-person sessions offer a dedicated space away from home and work, which many people find helps them settle in and open up. Online therapy can save a commute on days when fatigue, nausea, or a packed schedule make leaving the house hard. Many people find that[combining online and in-person sessions](https://lifestance.com/blog/online-therapy-vs-in-person-advice-from-therapists-who-provide-both/) gives them the best of both, so it is worth asking a provider which options they offer.


#### Explore Group Therapy Options


For some moms-to-be, connecting with others who are going through the same changes can be a comfort all its own.[Group therapy](https://lifestance.com/blog/group-therapy-vs-support-group-whats-right-for-you/) brings together a small group led by a licensed therapist, offering a place to share experiences, learn new coping skills, and to realize you are not alone.


#### Get the Right Level of Care


Every pregnancy is different, so there is no one-size-fits-all approach to mental health care. For some moms, a set of therapy sessions may be enough; for others, care may also include a[psychiatrist](https://lifestance.com/provider/psychiatrist/) to discuss whether[medication management](https://lifestance.com/psychiatric-medication/) makes sense. Encouragingly, care can make a measurable difference: a[study of thousands of LifeStance patients](https://lifestance.com/insight/depression-anxiety-treatment-outcomes/) found that 79% showed clinically significant improvement in anxiety symptoms and 73% experienced clinically significant improvement in depression symptoms compared to where they started.


Making therapy a priority during pregnancy may feel like one more item on a long list. But it may be one of the most meaningful ways to care for yourself, and for the little one on the way.
